parts.title: The teddy bear I could not lose
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
When I was four, my grandfather gave me a brown teddy bear with one ear missing. I called him Mr Button, because he had a red button instead of an eye. I took him everywhere, to the shops, to the beach and even to the dentist.

Once, when I was six, we went on holiday to Spain. At the airport, I put Mr Button down for a moment, and when I looked again, he was gone. I cried so much that my father went to every desk in the building. After an hour, a cleaner appeared with the bear in her hand. I have never been so happy in my life.

As I grew older, Mr Button spent more time on a shelf. At fourteen, I was embarrassed to have him in my room when friends visited, so I put him in a box.

Last month, I found him again while I was moving to a new flat. His red button was still shiny. I put him on my bed, and when my friends came to dinner, none of them laughed. One of them said that she still had her toy rabbit. Now Mr Button sits proudly on the sofa.

options: He had a red button eye
His ear looked like a button
questions.explanation: He had a red button instead of an eye.

options: He was lost at the airport
He was sent home by post
questions.explanation: He disappeared at the airport.

questions.explanation: A cleaner appeared with the bear in her hand.

questions.explanation: At fourteen she was embarrassed when friends visited.

parts.title: Toys through the ages
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
Children have always played with toys. [1] Archaeologists have found small clay animals and dolls in graves that are four thousand years old.

In the past, most toys were made at home. [2] Fathers carved wooden horses, and mothers made dolls from cloth.

In the nineteenth century, factories began to produce toys in large numbers. [3] Suddenly, even poor families could afford a doll or a spinning top.

Plastic arrived in the 1950s and changed everything. [4] The new toys were cheaper, brighter and almost impossible to break.

Today, many toys use electronics and can talk, move or connect to the internet. [5] Even so, simple things such as wooden blocks and balls remain as popular as ever.
sentences: Toys have been enjoyed by almost everyone.
Teddy bears became popular in the early twentieth century.
The oldest ones may have been used in religious ceremonies.
Both were made of wood and cost very little.
Factories could shape it into any form.
Some experts worry that children play outside less.

gaps.explanation: The oldest toys may have been ceremonial; the next sentence gives finds from graves.
Parents used whatever they had; the next sentence gives fathers carving horses.
Prices dropped; the next sentence says even poor families could afford toys.
Factories could shape plastic into any form; the next sentence says the new toys were cheaper.
Some experts worry about outdoor play; the next sentence says simple toys remain popular.

parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: Every year, our town holds a toy exchange. Children bring old toys that they do not play with any more [1] swap them for different ones. It is a clever idea, because nothing is wasted, and nobody spends a penny. This year, more than two hundred children came, [2] the hall was full of games, dolls and books. A girl called Moss swapped her bicycle helmet [3] a puzzle with five hundred pieces. She said that she had never had one before. Some children arrived early to make sure that they [4] the best toys. The organisers think that next year they will need a bigger hall, [5] the event is becoming so popular. Anyone can take part, [6] long as the toys are clean and not broken.

Make sure they got the best toys.
Because gives the reason: the event is becoming popular.

turns.speaker: a

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Yes! My aunt sent it as a birthday gift. It came in a lovely box with a card, but that’s not why I like it.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Was it expensive? It looks like it was.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: I think so. Mum said it cost nearly a hundred pounds, which is crazy. I don’t mind about that. The reason is that it can walk and talk. Yesterday it fell over and said "Oops, I’m tired", and I couldn’t stop laughing.

turns.speaker: a

turns.speaker: b

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Well, she gave it to me last year, but it wasn’t hers first. She thought it came from her aunt, so she asked her, and her aunt said no, she only kept it in a box.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: So who had it before?

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: It belonged to my gran’s mother, so she’s my great-gran. She got it for Christmas when she was seven, nearly a hundred years ago. Gran has a photograph with the doll on her lap.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Amazing. It looks very good for its age.

turns.speaker: b

I think it’s lovely, and it’s only fifteen pounds, so the price is fine too. What bothers me is the weather. The forecast for Saturday says light wind, and a big kite needs a good breeze. But two kings and a bishop were missing, so that was the end of that. Then we went outside to play football, but it started to rain after ten minutes. So we went back in, and Grandpa took out a pack of cards that he has had for forty years. We played until dinner, and I lost four times! Call me back and tell me about your weekend.

parts.title: A talk by a toy museum guide
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to the Toy Museum. I’m Dorota, and I’ll be your guide today. Before we start, a little history. Many people think that the museum is very old, but it isn’t. A collector called Mr Grey started it in his garage in nineteen eighty-five, and the doors opened to the public five years later, in nineteen ninety. When it opened, we had about four thousand toys. Today we have more than six thousand, and we receive new gifts every month. Now, our most famous object. You’ll see it in the first room, in the glass case. People always ask if it’s the old clay duck from Egypt. That’s the second oldest, and it’s about three thousand years old. The oldest one is a wooden horse with wheels, almost four thousand years old. Children pulled it along the street. Isn’t that lovely? The museum has three floors. On the ground floor, you will find the dolls and the dolls’ houses. Many visitors ask for the video games, and they are at the top, on the third floor. But the thing most people want is the model trains, and they are on the second floor, by the window. There’s a big switch that you can press, so don’t be shy. If you’d like to try something, the activity room is next to the shop. It opens at ten in the morning, and I know that the café closes at five, but the activity room is different. It closes at three, because the teachers come then to clean and prepare for tomorrow. So please go early. Everything is free. Finally, a few rules. You can take photos, and you can bring a small tripod if it’s not in the way. But please don’t use the flash. Light can damage old paint and cloth, and the guards will ask you to stop. Please also keep your food in the café. If you have any questions, ask any of us. We wear green shirts. Now, shall we begin with the horse?

gaps.prompt: The year of the first public visits: ___
gaps.explanation: Mr Grey started the museum in nineteen eighty-five, but it opened to the public five years later, in nineteen ninety.

gaps.prompt: Toys in the collection today: more than ___
gaps.explanation: They had about four thousand when it opened; now there are more than six thousand.

gaps.prompt: The most ancient item in the collection is a ___ with wheels
gaps.explanation: The clay duck is the second oldest; the oldest is a wooden horse with wheels.

gaps.prompt: The railway models are on the ___ floor
gaps.explanation: The dolls are on the ground floor and the video games on the third; the model trains are on the second floor.

gaps.prompt: Last activities in the workshop room end at ___
gaps.explanation: It opens at ten and the café closes at five, but the activity room closes at three.

gaps.prompt: Photos are fine, but do not switch on the ___
gaps.explanation: Small tripods are allowed, but the guards ask visitors to stop using the flash.

parts.title: An interview with a toy designer
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Holt, thank you for coming. Where do your ideas come from?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: People think I read about toys, and I do look at magazines, but they are all full of the same things. Visiting shops helps a little, to see the prices. The best way is to sit in a park or a nursery and watch children play. They use a box as a car and a spoon as a microphone, and that tells me more than any report.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Your most successful toy was a drawing box, wasn’t it? Why did it do so well?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Yes, and I’m still surprised. It wasn’t cheap, and no celebrity had one, so nobody paid for an advert. It sold well because children found so many ways to use it. It was a table, a house, even a boat. Parents told me that it was the toy that lasted longest at home.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Not every toy is a success. What about the talking robot?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Oh, the robot. It cost a lot to make and the shops sold only a few. People expect me to be furious or ashamed, and I can understand that, but I wasn’t. I stayed relaxed, honestly. I learned that children prefer to talk themselves than to listen to a toy. So it was a useful lesson.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: How long does it take to make a toy, from the first idea?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Much longer than people think. Not a few weeks, that’s only for the drawings. A simple toy needs about a year and a half, with models, tests and the factory. Eight years would be too long, but a big toy with electronics can take almost that.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Who tests your toys?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: We have a group of children from three to eight years old. Teachers sometimes give me their opinion, and I send parents a form, but I don’t trust that so much. Children can’t lie, and they never try to be polite. They tell you with their faces, and sometimes with a loud "no". If they put the toy down after two minutes, I know it’s not good.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: And finally, you still keep a wooden train. Why?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: It’s not worth much money, and to be fair it doesn’t work well any more. The wheels are loose. But I built it with my grandfather when I was six, using his tools. Every time I look at it, I remember his workshop. That’s the reason I never sell it, even when collectors offer me a good price. Some things are not for sale.

questions.explanation: Magazines are full of the same things and shops only show prices; the best way is to watch children play.
